★★★ THE RUNNABLE WITNESS FOR A SIGN THAT WAS SILENTLY DROPPED — D-ASM-NEGATIVE-SCALAR-LOSES-ITS-SIGN, shipped in `e5b60f6c` and found 2026-08-13.

★★★ WHY THIS EXAMPLE EXISTS AT ALL, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH READING. The defect lived for a full cycle behind a unit tier that was otherwise thorough: `tests/asm/test_asm_text_to_lir.cpp` had 43 tests over this walker, several of them asserting encoded BYTES, and not one of them wrote a negative number. The walker happily produced a well-formed LIR module, the assembler happily encoded it, the linker happily linked it, every leg was green — and the program computed the wrong answer. A corpus example whose EXIT CODE depends on the value is the instrument that catches that class, and this is it.

★★ WHAT EACH HALF PINS, AND WHY THEY ARE BOTH HERE.
  • The IMMEDIATE half (`movq $-8, %rcx`) is the plain case: `100 + (-8)` must be 92, and a dropped sign makes it 108. ⚠ It is DEPENDENT arithmetic on purpose — a program that merely `movq $-8, %rax; ret` would exit 248 either way on a byte-truncating exit status, and would prove nothing.
  • The DISPLACEMENT half (`movq %r9, -8(%rdx)`) is the strictly worse case: the dropped sign produces a WRONG ADDRESS, not a wrong constant. rsp+24 is poisoned with 1 and the store must clear it; if the store lands on rsp+40 instead, the poison survives and is added in. ✔MEASURED: on the pre-fix binary this arm alone moved the answer by exactly 1, which is why the two halves are given different magnitudes.

★ THE FOUR OUTCOMES ARE ALL DISTINCT — 92 correct · 108 immediate-sign dropped · 93 displacement-sign dropped · 109 both — so a partial regression cannot be read as a partial pass. That separation is deliberate: the first draft used the same magnitude for both halves and would have reported 100 for a single-half break AND for a double-half break with opposite errors.

★ THE FRAME IS HAND-WRITTEN because that is what the `encode` tier means: `subq $64, %rsp` / `addq $64, %rsp` is the programmer's own prologue and epilogue, and `materializeCallingConvention` does not run here by design. 64 keeps %rsp 16-byte aligned, and both touched slots (rsp+24, rsp+40) sit ABOVE the 32-byte region Win64 reserves as callee shadow space, so the same file is correct under both ABIs. ⚠ `-8(%rdx)` is computed from `leaq 32(%rsp), %rdx` rather than written as `-8(%rsp)` ON PURPOSE: a negative displacement off %rsp addresses the red zone, which System V permits and Windows does not, and this file must be correct on both.

★ ONLY REGISTERS VOLATILE UNDER *BOTH* ABIs ARE TOUCHED — rax, rcx, rdx, r8, r9. rsi/rdi would be the natural System V choice and are CALLEE-SAVED on Win64; using them yields a fixture that passes on Linux and corrupts the trampoline's state on Windows.

★ THE `release` ARM, SCOPED HONESTLY. At the `encode` tier no MIR module exists, so the optimizer, the register allocator and calling-convention materialization never run — this arm does NOT witness the optimizer and cannot. It pins the narrower fact that `--config=release` still produces a working binary from assembly text.

Legs actually run: windows/pe64-x86_64 and linux/elf64 (x86_64 + aarch64 under qemu); the darwin/macho64 leg was NOT run. Where the image is identical the arm's exit-code/stdout comparison is x==x and cannot fail. HONEST BY CONSTRUCTION: the source of this example IS assembly, so it is assembled without ever forming the HIR/MIR an optimizer pass runs on. No pipeline can transform it and no edit to this example could ever make this arm differ — the arm still earns its place by pinning that naming a pipeline does not BREAK an assembly example. Deliberately NOT given "mustDifferFromBaseline" — an honest no-op, not a missed opt-in.
